Article 33Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

1.In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where the notification to the supervisory authority is not made within 72 hours, it shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay.

2.The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.

3.The notification referred to in paragraph 1 shall at least:

(a)describe the nature of the personal data breach including where possible, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of personal data records concerned;

(b)communicate the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point where more information can be obtained;

(c)describe the likely consequences of the personal data breach;

(d)describe the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the controller to address the personal data breach, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects.

4.Where, and in so far as, it is not possible to provide the information at the same time, the information may be provided in phases without undue further delay.

5.The controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts relating to the personal data breach, its effects and the remedial action taken. That documentation shall enable the supervisory authority to verify compliance with this Article.

EUR-Lex
Obligations for data controllers
If your SME acts as a data controller, there are three primary principles regarding data breaches
documentation of any personal data breaches
notification of any personal data breach to the relevant data protection authority (DPA) within 72 hours,  unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals; and
communication of that breach to the individuals without undue delay, where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to individuals.
It is of utmost importance that data controllers understand and comply with these obligations, and implement in advance the appropriate procedures that will allow them to objectively determine in due time whether any of the notifications mentioned above are required.
In any event, for all breaches – even those that are not notified to a DPA, on the basis that they have been assessed as being unlikely to result in a risk – the data controller must record at least the basic details of the breach, the assessment thereof, its effects, and the steps taken in response, as required by Art. 33(5) GDPR.

Similarly, per Art. 33(2) GDPR, if your SME is a data processor, processing personal data on behalf of another organisation, you must notify the data controller of any personal data breach without undue delay. This is of key importance in enabling the data controller to comply with their notification obligations in due time. A notification of a personal data breach to the relevant DPA must at least:

communicate the name and contact details of the data protection officer (DPO) or other contact point where more information can be obtained;
describe the likely consequences of the personal data breach; and
describe the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the SME to address the personal data breach, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects.

# Data-protection clauses — UK controller / EU processor supplier agreement

**Status:** Draft for review by a qualified attorney. Not legal advice.

**Jurisdiction and roles (assumed, challenge if wrong):** The customer is a company incorporated in the United Kingdom (England and Wales assumed) and is the **controller**. The supplier is established in a Member State of the European Union and is the **processor**. Both the UK GDPR and the EU GDPR are addressed. A rule of one instrument is not assumed to hold in the other without citation; on the sources below, Articles 28(2), 28(3) and 33(2) are in identical terms in both.

---

## A. Finding on the processor breach-notification deadline (asks 3 and 4)

The deadline that actually applies to a **processor** is **not a number of hours**. It is the statutory standard **"without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach"**.

**Instruments and articles, cited in full:**

1. **Article 33(2) of the UK GDPR** — Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), as it forms part of the law of the United Kingdom, as amended by the Data Protection, Privacy and Electronic Communications (Amendments etc) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (S.I. 2019/419). Text at legislation.gov.uk, Article 33: "The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach."

2. **Article 33(2) of the EU GDPR** — Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (Text with EEA relevance). Identical words: "The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach."

**The 72-hour figure is not the processor deadline.** Article 33(1) of each instrument imposes on the **controller** a duty to notify the competent supervisory authority "without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it", unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. That duty does not apply to the processor.

**Ask 4 is not triggered.** The deadline has been established from the primary sources quoted above. It is therefore **not marked blocking**. What would be blocking — and what this draft refuses to do — is to write a plausible number of hours (24, 48 or 72) into the processor clause as if the regulation prescribed it. The regulation does not.

Official secondary confirmation (not relied on in place of the articles): European Data Protection Board, SME guidance, *Assess the risks / Data breaches*: "per Art. 33(2) GDPR, if your SME is a data processor … you must notify the data controller of any personal data breach without undue delay"; and "The requirements on breach reporting should also be detailed in the contract between the data controller and processor, as required under Art. 28 GDPR."

---

## B. Operative clauses

Insert as **Schedule [•] — Data Protection** to the supplier agreement, or as the data-protection section of that agreement. Square brackets mark facts or commercial choices for the reviewing attorney. Defined terms below control.

### Part 1 — Definitions and interpretation

**1.1 Definitions.** In this Schedule:

- **"Applicable Data Protection Law"** means any data protection or privacy law applicable to the Processing of Personal Data under the Agreement, including: (a) the **UK GDPR** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as it forms part of the law of the United Kingdom, as amended by the Data Protection, Privacy and Electronic Communications (Amendments etc) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (S.I. 2019/419)); (b) the **Data Protection Act 2018** (c. 12); (c) the **EU GDPR** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016); and (d) any applicable implementing or supplementary legislation of an EU Member State; in each case as amended, replaced or superseded.
- **"Controller"** means the UK company party to the Agreement, being the controller in respect of the Personal Data.
- **"EU GDPR"** means Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (Text with EEA relevance).
- **"Personal Data"**, **"Personal Data Breach"**, **"Processing"**, **"Supervisory Authority"** and **"Sub-Processor"** have the meanings given in Applicable Data Protection Law.
- **"Processor"** means the EU-established supplier party to the Agreement, being the processor in respect of the Personal Data.
- **"Services"** means the services supplied by the Processor under the Agreement.
- **"UK GDPR"** means Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as it forms part of the law of the United Kingdom, as amended by S.I. 2019/419 and applied by the Data Protection Act 2018.

**1.2 Interpretation.** Headings are for convenience only. References to Articles are to articles of the UK GDPR or, where the EU GDPR applies to the Processing, the corresponding article of the EU GDPR (which, in respect of Articles 28 and 33, is the same numbered article in identical terms on the sources cited in section A). A reference to a statute or regulation includes that instrument as amended or replaced.

### Part 2 — Roles, scope and processing purposes (ask 2)

**2.1 Roles.** The Controller determines the purposes and means of the Processing. The Processor Processes Personal Data only as a processor on behalf of the Controller. The Processor shall not determine the purposes and means of the Processing. If the Processor does so, it shall be considered a controller in respect of that Processing (Article 28(10), UK GDPR; Article 28(10), EU GDPR) and shall so notify the Controller without delay.

**2.2 Details of Processing.** The subject-matter, duration, nature and purpose of the Processing, the type of Personal Data and the categories of data subjects are set out in **Schedule 1**. The Parties shall keep Schedule 1 current. Processing is limited to what is set out in Schedule 1 and to the Controller's documented instructions.

**2.3 Processing purposes.** The Processor shall Process Personal Data solely for the purposes of performing the Services in accordance with the Agreement and the Controller's documented instructions, and for no other purpose. Without limitation, the Processor shall not Process Personal Data for the Processor's own purposes, including the Processor's product development, service improvement, benchmarking, analytics for the Processor's own benefit, or the training, tuning or evaluation of any model (including any machine-learning or artificial-intelligence model), except to the extent expressly authorised in a documented instruction.

**2.4 Documented instructions.** The Processor shall Process Personal Data only on documented instructions from the Controller, including with regard to transfers of Personal Data to a third country or an international organisation, unless required to do so by Applicable Data Protection Law to which the Processor is subject; in that case the Processor shall inform the Controller of that legal requirement before Processing, unless that law prohibits such information on important grounds of public interest (Article 28(3)(a), UK GDPR; Article 28(3)(a), EU GDPR). The Agreement, this Schedule and Schedule 1 constitute the Controller's initial documented instructions. Additional instructions shall be given in writing (including email).

**2.5 Duration.** The Processing continues for the term of the Services and thereafter only as permitted by Part 6 (deletion or return) or as required by Applicable Data Protection Law.

**2.6 Sufficiency of guarantees.** The Processor warrants that it provides sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in such a manner that Processing will meet the requirements of Applicable Data Protection Law and ensure the protection of the rights of the data subject (Article 28(1), UK GDPR; Article 28(1), EU GDPR).

### Part 3 — Processor obligations (Article 28(3) stipulations)

**3.1 Confidentiality.** The Processor shall ensure that persons authorised to Process the Personal Data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality (Article 28(3)(b)).

**3.2 Security.** The Processor shall take all measures required pursuant to Article 32 of the UK GDPR and Article 32 of the EU GDPR (security of processing), having regard to the state of the art, the costs of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purposes of Processing, and the risk. The measures in force at the start of the Services are described in **[Schedule 2 / the Processor's security exhibit]**. The Processor shall not materially diminish those measures without the Controller's prior written consent.

**3.3 Data-subject rights.** Taking into account the nature of the Processing, the Processor shall assist the Controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the Controller's obligation to respond to requests for exercising the data subject's rights laid down in Chapter III (Article 28(3)(e)). The Processor shall notify the Controller without undue delay if it receives a request from a data subject in respect of the Personal Data, and shall not respond unless instructed to do so by the Controller or required by Applicable Data Protection Law.

**3.4 Articles 32 to 36.** Taking into account the nature of Processing and the information available to the Processor, the Processor shall assist the Controller in ensuring compliance with Articles 32 to 36 (Article 28(3)(f)), including security, Personal Data Breach notification to the Supervisory Authority and to data subjects, data-protection impact assessment, and prior consultation.

**3.5 Information and audit.** The Processor shall make available to the Controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with Article 28 and shall allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the Controller or another auditor mandated by the Controller (Article 28(3)(h)). Audits shall be conducted on reasonable notice, during business hours, so as to minimise disruption, and subject to reasonable confidentiality and security conditions. The Processor may satisfy this clause by providing regularly updated independent audit reports and certifications where those reports cover the relevant systems.

**3.6 Records.** The Processor shall maintain records of Processing activities as required by Article 30(2) of the UK GDPR and Article 30(2) of the EU GDPR, and shall make them available to the Controller on request.

**3.7 Form.** This Schedule forms part of a contract in writing (including electronic form) as required by Article 28(9), UK GDPR, and Article 28(9), EU GDPR.

### Part 4 — Sub-processor consent mechanism (ask 2)

**4.1 Prior written authorisation.** The Processor shall not engage another processor (a **Sub-Processor**) without prior specific or general written authorisation of the Controller (Article 28(2), UK GDPR; Article 28(2), EU GDPR).

**4.2 General written authorisation.** The Controller hereby gives **general written authorisation** for the Processor to engage the Sub-Processors listed in **Schedule 3** for the Processing described in Schedule 1, subject to this Part 4. Engagement of any other Sub-Processor requires the Controller's prior specific written authorisation.

**4.3 Notice of change.** In the case of the general written authorisation in clause 4.2, the Processor shall inform the Controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of Sub-Processors, thereby giving the Controller the opportunity to object to such changes (Article 28(2)). The Processor shall give that information in writing (email sufficient) at least **[14]** days before the intended engagement. **[The 14-day period is a commercial term; Article 28(2) does not fix the length of the notice or objection period.]**

**4.4 Objection.** The Controller may object to an intended addition or replacement by written notice within **[14]** days of receipt of the Processor's information. If the Controller objects:

- (a) the Processor shall not engage the objected-to Sub-Processor for the Controller's Personal Data;
- (b) the Parties shall discuss in good faith a reasonably practicable alternative; and
- (c) if no reasonably practicable alternative exists and the Processor cannot perform the Services without the Sub-Processor, either Party may terminate the affected Services on written notice, without prejudice to any other right.

**4.5 Flow-down.** Where a Sub-Processor is engaged, the Processor shall impose on the Sub-Processor, by way of a written contract, the same data-protection obligations as are imposed on the Processor by this Schedule, in particular the obligations in Article 28(3) (Article 28(4)). The Processor shall remain fully liable to the Controller for the performance of that Sub-Processor's obligations (Article 28(4), final sentence).

**4.6 Specific authorisation fallback.** If the Controller prefers **specific** authorisation for every Sub-Processor (the alternative permitted by Article 28(2)), delete clauses 4.2 to 4.4 and substitute: "The Processor shall not engage any Sub-Processor without the Controller's prior specific written authorisation in each case."

**4.7 Emergency.** If Applicable Data Protection Law or an emergency reasonably requires a Sub-Processor to be engaged before the notice period in clause 4.3 can expire, the Processor may do so only if it notifies the Controller as soon as reasonably practicable and the engagement is otherwise authorised under this Part 4. The Controller's objection rights continue to apply.

### Part 5 — Personal data breach notification (asks 2, 3 and 4)

**5.1 Statutory deadline — without undue delay.** If a Personal Data Breach occurs, the Processor shall notify the Controller **without undue delay after becoming aware of** the Personal Data Breach.

That is the deadline that applies to a processor under:

- **Article 33(2) of the UK GDPR** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as it forms part of the law of the United Kingdom, as amended by S.I. 2019/419); and
- **Article 33(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016** (the EU GDPR).

The words of Article 33(2) in each instrument are: *"The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach."*

**5.2 No numeric processor deadline; 72 hours is a controller duty.** The Parties record that neither the UK GDPR nor the EU GDPR prescribes a fixed period of hours or days within which a **processor** must notify the **controller**. The applicable statutory deadline is "without undue delay after becoming aware", as set out in clause 5.1. The **72-hour** period in **Article 33(1)** of each instrument is the deadline (where feasible) for a **controller** to notify the competent supervisory authority; it is **not** a deadline for the Processor. Nothing in this Part 5 converts Article 33(1) into a processor deadline.

**5.3 Manner of notice.** Notice under clause 5.1 shall be given to the Controller's breach contact in Schedule 1 (or such other contact as the Controller designates in writing), by telephone **and** email, and shall be followed as soon as the Processor is reasonably able by a written notice containing the matters in clause 5.4.

**5.4 Content of notice.** The written notice shall, so far as the Processor is then able, include:

- (a) the nature of the Personal Data Breach, including where possible the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of Personal Data records concerned;
- (b) the name and contact details of the Processor's data protection officer or other contact point where more information can be obtained;
- (c) the likely consequences of the Personal Data Breach; and
- (d) the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the Processor to address the Personal Data Breach, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects.

These matters correspond to Article 33(3). Where it is not possible to provide the information at the same time, the information may be provided in phases without undue further delay (cf. Article 33(4)).

**5.5 Cooperation with the Controller's Article 33(1) duty.** The Parties acknowledge that the Controller may be required, under Article 33(1) of the UK GDPR and/or Article 33(1) of the EU GDPR, to notify a Supervisory Authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the Controller has become aware of a Personal Data Breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. To enable the Controller to assess and, where required, make that notification, the Processor shall provide the information in clause 5.4 as promptly as practicable. Any additional contractual cut-off the Parties may agree (see the drafting note after this Schedule) is an overlay; it is not the statutory processor deadline.

**5.6 No unilateral external notification.** The Processor shall not notify any Supervisory Authority or any data subject in respect of a Personal Data Breach unless instructed to do so by the Controller in writing or required to do so by Applicable Data Protection Law. If required by law, the Processor shall, to the extent lawful, consult the Controller before doing so.

**5.7 Documentation.** The Processor shall document each Personal Data Breach, comprising the facts relating to the breach, its effects and the remedial action taken, and shall make that documentation available to the Controller on reasonable request.

**5.8 Awareness.** For the purposes of clause 5.1, the Processor is "aware" of a Personal Data Breach when it has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has occurred that has led to Personal Data being compromised, lost, stolen, wrongly disclosed, altered or otherwise breached, or when a Sub-Processor has so notified the Processor.

### Part 6 — Deletion or return at termination (ask 2)

**6.1 Controller's election.** After the end of the provision of Services relating to Processing, the Processor shall, at the choice of the Controller, **delete** or **return** all the Personal Data, and delete existing copies, unless Applicable Data Protection Law requires storage of the Personal Data (Article 28(3)(g), UK GDPR; Article 28(3)(g), EU GDPR). In the UK GDPR the words of Article 28(3)(g) as amended by S.I. 2019/419, Sch. 1 para. 22(2)(c), refer to storage required by "domestic law"; in the EU GDPR the corresponding words refer to "Union or Member State law". This clause uses "Applicable Data Protection Law" to cover both.

**6.2 How the election is made.** The Controller shall make the election by written notice given before or within **[30]** days after termination or expiry of the affected Services. If the Controller does not make an election in that period, the Processor shall delete the Personal Data in accordance with clause 6.4, unless clause 6.6 applies. **[The 30-day election window is a commercial term; Article 28(3)(g) does not fix it.]**

**6.3 Return.** If the Controller elects return, the Processor shall return the Personal Data to the Controller in a reasonable, commonly used, machine-readable format identified by the Parties, by secure means, and shall not retain copies except as permitted by clause 6.6.

**6.4 Deletion.** If the Controller elects deletion (or is treated as having done so under clause 6.2), the Processor shall delete all Personal Data, including existing copies, using methods appropriate to the medium and consistent with Article 32, so that the Personal Data cannot reasonably be reconstructed.

**6.5 Timing.** Deletion or return shall be completed without undue delay after the election (or after the end of the Services, if earlier), and in any event within **[30]** days after the election. **[The 30-day completion period is a commercial term.]**

**6.6 Retention carve-outs.** The Processor may retain Personal Data to the extent and for so long as:

- (a) Applicable Data Protection Law requires storage of that Personal Data (Article 28(3)(g)); or
- (b) the Controller has notified a binding legal hold in writing.

Retained Personal Data remains subject to this Schedule, shall be isolated and not otherwise Processed, and shall be deleted when the requirement ends.

**6.7 Backups.** Where deletion from backup media is not immediately technically possible, the Processor shall (a) suspend active use of the backup copies, (b) apply the confidentiality and security restrictions in this Schedule until deletion is complete, and (c) delete the backup copies in accordance with the Processor's backup overwrite cycle, not exceeding **[90]** days after the deletion obligation arises. **[The 90-day backup cap is a commercial term.]**

**6.8 Certification.** Within **[30]** days after completing deletion or return, the Processor shall provide a written certificate, signed by an authorised representative, confirming: the action taken (deletion, return, or both in part); the date of completion; the systems and locations covered; any Personal Data retained under clause 6.6 or 6.7 and the legal basis; and that existing copies have been deleted except as so retained. **[The 30-day certification window is a commercial term.]**

**6.9 Survival.** Parts 1, 3.1, 5, 6 and 8 survive termination or expiry of the Agreement for so long as the Processor retains any Personal Data.

### Part 7 — Transfers

**7.1 Instructions.** The Processor shall not transfer Personal Data outside the United Kingdom or the European Economic Area except on the Controller's documented instructions or as required by Applicable Data Protection Law (Article 28(3)(a)).

**7.2 Mechanism.** The Parties shall put in place any transfer mechanism required by Applicable Data Protection Law for any restricted transfer. **[DRAFTING NOTE — not established from the materials provided: the correct tool for UK→EEA or onward transfers (IDTA, UK Addendum to EU SCCs, adequacy regulations, or other), and the interaction of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, Sch. 9 with pre-commencement standard clauses, are left for the reviewing attorney. No transfer tool is inserted here.]**

### Part 8 — Miscellaneous

**8.1 Supervisory Authorities.** The Processor shall promptly notify the Controller of any communication from a Supervisory Authority relating to the Personal Data, unless legally prohibited.

**8.2 Order of precedence.** If there is a conflict, this Schedule prevails over the body of the Agreement in respect of the Processing of Personal Data, except that nothing in this Schedule limits a Party's liability where the Agreement provides that data-protection liability cannot be limited.

**8.3 No determination of purposes.** Without prejudice to clause 2.1, the Processor shall not, by determining the purposes and means of Processing, cause Article 28(10) to apply.

**8.4 Liability.** Liability, indemnities and limitation of liability are dealt with in [clause •] of the Agreement. **[DRAFTING NOTE: not drafted here; outside the four requested topics.]**

## E. Drafting notes for the reviewing attorney

1. **Processor deadline — do not insert hours.** The operative clause (5.1–5.2) states the actual statutory deadline ("without undue delay after becoming aware") and names Article 33(2) of each instrument. If the client wants a contractual cut-off so the controller can meet Article 33(1)'s 72-hour SA notification, add a clause of the form: "The Processor shall give the notice in clause 5.1 within [48] hours of becoming aware." Label it expressly as a **contractual overlay**, not as the regulation's processor deadline. Do not describe that number as the deadline "under the regulation".
2. **Sub-processor model.** General authorisation with objection is drafted (Article 28(2) permits general or specific). The 14-day notice/objection periods are commercial. Switch to specific authorisation via clause 4.6 if the client requires it.
3. **Purposes and data categories.** Schedule 1 is a placeholder. The purposes clause (2.3) is drafted tightly and excludes processor-side analytics and model training unless expressly instructed.
4. **Deletion vs return.** Article 28(3)(g) gives the choice to the controller. Commercial timings ([30]/[90] days) are marked as such. Certification is a contractual addition, not an Article 28 requirement.
5. **Both regimes.** The clauses are written to satisfy Article 28 of the UK GDPR and Article 28 of the EU GDPR. If instructions confirm only one regime applies, the dual citations can be simplified; until then they should stay.
6. **Transfers.** Not resolved from the materials. See clause 7.2. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, Sch. 9, Pt 2 (transitional treatment of pre-commencement standard clauses and adequacy regulations under the reformed UK GDPR Chapter 5) was reviewed; it does not itself supply the operative transfer tool for this agreement.
7. **Article 28(3) completeness.** Parts 2–3 and 6 together stipulate the matters required by Article 28(3)(a)–(h) and the writing requirement in Article 28(9), so the Schedule is a complete Article 28 contract and not only the four requested topics.
